news.summary:
Exclusive: Lewisham council’s move marks first step in Greens’ plan to create a corridor of sanctuary boroughs across London

A Green-led London council is planning to ban its officials from working with the Home Office on immigration raids, after uncovering evidence suggesting government officials wanted to use environmental health data to target restaurant workers.

news_drafts.headline: Lewisham's capital spending surges 62% in three months, forcing major new borrowing
news_drafts.lead: Lewisham Council's four-year capital spending forecast jumped by £263m in three months, from £421m in March to £685m in June 2026, forcing the authority to shift from relying on its own cash reserves to active borrowing on the capital markets. The council will borrow £42m for general spending and £31m for housing in 2026–27 alone. The expansion, largely driven by the Building for Lewisham housing programme, comes as the council's liquid investment reserves have depleted by £54m in a year to £210m. Debt service costs are projected to rise from 4.8 per cent of the annual budget to 7.7 per cent by 2027–28, constraining spending flexibility. The council is borrowing at a time when interest rates remain stubbornly high: the Bank Rate is forecast to stay at 3.75 per cent or rise further, and long-term borrowing from the Public Works Loan Board costs 5.6 per cent over 25 years.

news_drafts.headline: Lewisham cuts pension contributions as £301m surplus grows
news_drafts.lead: Lewisham Council's pension contribution rate fell from 21.5 per cent of payroll to 17.6 per cent from 1 April 2026, releasing money for other services. The reduction follows a sharp improvement in the fund's finances. The 2025 triennial valuation — the three-yearly health check on the scheme — found the fund had enough assets to cover all pensions and still hold a surplus of £301m. In 2022 the fund was 97 per cent funded; it is now 119 per cent funded. This improvement prompted the lower contributions.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Outturn and Mid-Year Review 2026-27 Council
findings.headline: Investment reserves declining from £264m to £210m as council depletes cash to fund capital, reducing financial flexibility.
findings.detail: The council's liquid investment portfolio has shrunk by £54m from £264m (June 2025) to £210m (June 2026), and the yield has fallen from 4.3% to 3.7%. The council is deliberately running down these reserves as an alternative to borrowing for capital spend, but this strategy is being exhausted. As cash reserves deplete, the council will become increasingly reliant on capital markets borrowing. The document indicates investment returns will continue to fall as interest rates are expected to decline.
findings.matters: Declining cash reserves indicate the council is exhausting alternative funding options and will become entirely dependent on borrowed funding once reserves are depleted, removing its financial buffer and making it more vulnerable to adverse borrowing conditions or unexpected cost pressures.
findings.figures: Investments: £264m (June 2025) → £210m (June 2026), a decline of £54m; yield declining from 4.3% to 3.7%.
findings.quote: The current investments of £210m as at 30 June 2026 (£264m 2025) will give the Council a 3.7% return compared to 4.3% at June 2025.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Outturn and Mid-Year Review 2026-27 Council
findings.headline: LOBO loans reduced by £65m in two years (£119.7m to £54.3m), with further £17.5m repaid since April 2026, reducing refinancing risk.
findings.detail: The council has systematically reduced its LOBO (Lender's Option Borrower's Option) exposure from £119.7m to £54.3m over two years, plus an additional £17.5m repayment since April 2026. This brings the outstanding balance to approximately £36.8m. The council had been in correspondence with its LOBO lenders exploring rescheduling opportunities. This proactive reduction removes exposure to refinancing risk if lenders exercise their call option at higher rates.
findings.matters: LOBOs create refinancing risk at call dates; if exercised, the council must choose between repaying at par or accepting a new (potentially higher) rate. Reducing this exposure demonstrates sound risk management and reduces financial volatility from refinancing decisions outside the council's control.
findings.figures: LOBO loans: £119.7m (two years ago) → £54.3m (31 March 2026) → approximately £36.8m (post-April 2026); total reduction of £83m over two years.
findings.quote: In the last two years the Council has reduced its LOBO loans from £119.7m to £54.3m as at 31 March 2026. Since 1 April 2026 the Council has repaid a further £17.5m of LOBO loans.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Outturn and Mid-Year Review 2026-27 Council
findings.headline: Debt service cost ratio rising from 4.8% to 7.7% of net revenue by 2027/28 (excluding PFI), reducing budget flexibility.
findings.detail: The proportion of revenue consumed by debt service is projected to increase from 4.8% (2025/26 actual) to 6.0% (2026/27) and 7.7% (2027/28), representing a 2.9 percentage point increase by 2027/28. This rising trend means an increasing share of the council's annual budget is locked into servicing debt, leaving less flexibility for service delivery and less resilience to unexpected pressures.
findings.matters: A rising debt service ratio indicates increasing financial stress and eroding budget flexibility. Lenders track this closely as an indicator of whether the council can sustain its debt burden without compromising service delivery or requiring spending cuts.
findings.figures: Financing costs as percentage of net revenue (excl. PFI): 4.8% (2025/26 actual), 6.0% (2026/27 estimate), 7.7% (2027/28 estimate).
findings.quote: This indicator identifies the trend in the cost of borrowing for capital purposes, against the net revenue stream.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Outturn and Mid-Year Review 2026-27 Council
findings.headline: Capital programme jumped 62% in three months from £421.4m to £684.6m, forcing substantial new borrowing (£72.6m in 2026/27 alone).
findings.detail: Between March and June 2026, Lewisham's four-year capital programme forecast increased by £263.2m — a 62% rise. This forces the council to shift from its under-borrowing strategy to active borrowing. The council will need £42m general fund borrowing and £30.6m HRA borrowing in 2026/27. The bulk of the increase comes from the Housing Revenue Account, particularly the 'Building for Lewisham' programme.
findings.matters: A lender would need to understand what is driving such a large and rapid increase in capital plans, whether this reflects a sustained policy shift, and how sustainable the resulting additional borrowing will be for the council's medium-term finances.
findings.figures: Capital programme: £421.4m (March 2026 forecast) to £684.6m (June 2026 forecast); prudential borrowing requirement: £42.0m general fund and £30.6m HRA for 2026/27.
findings.quote: The Capital Programme for 2026-30 was agreed as £421.4m in March 2026 and is now forecast to be £684.6m as at 30 June 2026, an increase of £263.2m.

findings.headline: Rate forecast already acknowledged as likely to be revised upward due to inflation pressures and unforeseen geopolitical events
findings.detail: The MUFG forecast was made in June 2026, before the ceasefire in the Middle East was broken. The council explicitly states it expects MUFG to provide a revised forecast as inflation pressures grow, indicating the current forecast may quickly become obsolete.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence in financial projections; a council acknowledging that its rate forecast is likely to be revised upward within weeks suggests significant uncertainty about 2026-27 borrowing costs and the stability of treasury assumptions
findings.figures: Forecast made June 2026; Middle East conflict broke out after June; revision expected due to inflation
findings.quote: We expect MUFG to provide a revised forecast as pressure on inflation grows.
